affected_parts.quote: Young leaves become pale in colour and appear thin and narrow. As the disease progresses, all new tillers grow in white or yellow colour, giving the plant a grassy appearance. The affected clumps are stunted with premature proliferation of auxillary buds. If canes are formed, they appear thin with shorter internodes, having aerial roots at the lower nodes. The buds on such canes are usually papery and abnormally elongated.

summary.value: Numerous lanky tillers give the plant a bushy, grass-like appearance. Leaves become pale yellow to completely chlorotic, thin, and narrow, with stunted clumps and reduced internodes.
summary.quote: The disease is characterised by the production of numerous lanky tillers from the base of the affected shoots. Leaves become pale yellow to completely chlorotic, thin and narrow. The plants appear bushy and 'grass-like' due to reduction in the length of internodes premature and continuous tillering.

diagnostic_features.value: Bushy, grass-like appearance from excessive lanky tillering at the base; pale yellow to fully chlorotic, thin and narrow leaves; stunted clumps with premature proliferation of axillary buds; all new tillers grow white or yellow; secondary infection on full-grown canes shows side sprouting and yellowing; canes thin with shorter internodes and aerial roots at lower nodes; buds papery and abnormally elongated.
diagnostic_features.quote: The plants appear bushy and 'grass-like' due to reduction in the length of internodes premature and continuous tillering. The affected clumps are stunted with premature proliferation of auxillary buds. Cane formation rarely occurs in the affected clumps, if formed, thin with shorter internodes having aerial roots at the lower nodes. The buds on such canes usually papery and abnormally elongated.

look_alikes.quote: The symptoms have similarities with those of iron deficiency but appear in random, isolated areas on your field.

conflicts.note: Plantix classifies the causal agent under 'Bacteria' but the pathogen is named 'Sugarcane grassy shoot phytoplasma'; phytoplasmas are prokaryotes formerly grouped with bacteria but are now treated separately. The eAgri/TNAU source explicitly states 'Phytoplasma' as the causal agent.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Pathogenicity assay confirmed that F. verticillioides was directly responsible for disease on sugarcane.

type_of_disease.quote: Identification and Characterization of Pathogenic and Endophytic Fungal Species Associated with Pokkah Boeng Disease of Sugarcane

affected_parts.quote: Diseased plants were observed for the following symptoms: leaf malformation, leaf curling, stalk rot, red streaking, and necrosis.

summary.value: Chlorotic patches on young leaves, leaf malformation and distortion, top rot with dried spindle base, transverse knife-cut marks on stalks, red streaking, and stalk rot with necrosis.
summary.quote: Malformation and distortion of the top or damaged stalk. Appearance of chlorotic patches towards the base of young leaves.

diagnostic_features.value: Three distinct phases: (1) chlorotic patches at base of young leaves with wrinkled, twisted, shortened leaves; (2) top rot phase with pronounced malformation, red specks dissolved, spindle base rotten and dried; (3) knife cut stage with transverse cuts in the rind of the stalk visible when leaves are stripped off, revealing large conspicuous chlorotic patches on stalks; also red streaking and chlorosis on leaves, stalk rot with extensive tissue maceration.
diagnostic_features.quote: The disease develops in three major phases. The earliest symptoms are the appearance of chlorotic patches towards the base of young leaves and occasionally on other parts of the leaf blades in the first phase. Leaves are wrinkled, twisted and shortened. The top rot phase is the most serious stage where the malformation and twisting of leaves are pronounced. Red specks are dissolved and the whole base of the spindle gets rotten and dried up. The third stage known as the knife cut stage shows transverse cuts in the rind of the stalk or stem. When leaves are stripped off, large conspicuous chlorotic patches are seen on stalks.

conflicts.note: Fusarium moniliforme is an older synonym for Fusarium verticillioides. The peer-reviewed PMC article (higher authority) names F. verticillioides as the confirmed pathogen via pathogenicity assay. Plantix uses the outdated name F. moniliforme.

type_of_disease.quote: The bacterium that causes leaf scald lives from year to year in infected plants.

affected_parts.quote: Leaves of young plants may show bleaching or yellowing. Under severe disease conditions, entire plants may die.

summary.value: Narrow white pencil lines running longitudinally along veins from the leaf margin down the blade into the sheath, with bands of dead tissue developing along these lines. Leaf tips dry out giving a scalded appearance; etiolated leaves; entire plants may die in severe cases.
summary.quote: The characteristic symptom of leaf scald is the presence of one or more narrow, white "pencil lines" running longitudinally along a vein from the leaf margin down the blade into the sheath. Bands of dead tissue then develop along pencil lines starting at the leaf margin and may expand until the entire leaf is dead.

diagnostic_features.value: Narrow white pencil lines running longitudinally along a vein from the leaf margin down the blade into the sheath, with bands of dead tissue developing along these lines.
diagnostic_features.quote: The characteristic symptom of leaf scald is the presence of one or more narrow, white "pencil lines" running longitudinally along a vein from the leaf margin down the blade into the sheath. Bands of dead tissue then develop along pencil lines starting at the leaf margin

conflicts.note: PlantVillage uses a misspelling 'Xanthomonas albileneans'; the correct spelling is Xanthomonas albilineans as used by LSU AgCenter.
PlantVillage only lists foliar; LSU AgCenter notes whole plant can be affected under severe conditions.

pathogen_scientific_name.value: Sugarcane mosaic virus; Sorghum mosaic virus
pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Mosaic (Sorghum mosaic virus and Sugarcane mosaic virus)

type_of_disease.quote: The virus persists from year to year in infected plants. It is spread primarily by migrating aphids

affected_parts.quote: there are many irregular yellow and green inlays, stripes, or mottles alternate with parallel veins on symptomatic leaves; they move quickly in vascular bundles, along with the flow of plant nutrients; the virus can spread to almost every tissue, even the whole stool

summary.value: Irregular yellow and green inlays, stripes, or mottles on leaves alternating with parallel veins; severely infected leaves turn yellow or yellow-white with green islets or red punctate necrosis; new leaf tips may be abnormally twisted. Symptoms most evident in youngest emerging leaves and young plants.
summary.quote: there are many irregular yellow and green inlays, stripes, or mottles alternate with parallel veins on symptomatic leaves, more clearly visible against the sunlight. Some are mostly normal green with only a few narrow pale-yellow streaks, some show very obvious whole leaf chlorosis, and the seriously infected leaves turn yellow or yellow white, leaving only a few green islets or a small amount of red punctate necrosis, or the tips of new leaves are abnormally twisted

diagnostic_features.value: Symptoms most visible in the middle and lower sections of new leaves; irregular yellow and green mosaic patterns alternate with parallel veins, more clearly visible against sunlight; some varieties show cryptic symptoms at high temperature that recur as temperature drops.
diagnostic_features.quote: The symptoms of mosaic disease caused by SCMV, SrMV and SCSMV are similar, especially in the middle and lower sections of new leaves. In comparison to healthy leaves, there are many irregular yellow and green inlays, stripes, or mottles alternate with parallel veins on symptomatic leaves, more clearly visible against the sunlight. Some varieties show cryptic or indistinct phenomena at a high temperature, but the symptoms recur as the temperature drops

look_alikes.quote: Symptoms were similar to another viral disease of St. Augustinegrass called St. Augustinegrass decline (SAD, caused by Panicum mosaic virus)

conflicts.note: LSU AgCenter lists only foliar; PMC article notes vascular and whole plant involvement

conflicts.canonical_value: Sugarcane mosaic virus; Sorghum mosaic virus
conflicts.note: UF IFAS EDIS source focuses solely on Sugarcane mosaic virus (SCMV); LSU AgCenter lists both SCMV and SrMV

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV) is one of the most widespread viruses causing disease in sugarcane worldwide.

type_of_disease.quote: Sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV) is one of the most widespread viruses causing disease in sugarcane worldwide.

affected_parts.quote: Infection with SCYLV results in intense yellowing of the midrib, which extends to the leaf blade, followed by tissue necrosis from the leaf tip towards the leaf base. ... SCYLV infection affects carbon assimilation and metabolism in sugarcane, resulting in stunted plants in severe cases.

summary.value: Intense yellowing of the leaf midrib extending to the leaf blade, followed by tissue necrosis progressing from the leaf tip toward the leaf base, with stunted plants in severe cases. The underside of the mid-vein on young leaves at the apex of mature plants turns bright yellow, spreading into the leaf blade; mid-veins can turn pink in severely infected plants.
summary.quote: Infection with SCYLV results in intense yellowing of the midrib, which extends to the leaf blade, followed by tissue necrosis from the leaf tip towards the leaf base.

diagnostic_features.value: Intense yellowing starting at the midrib and extending to the leaf blade, with necrosis progressing from the leaf tip toward the base; symptomatic leaves show increased respiration, reduced photosynthesis, altered hexose-to-sucrose ratio, and increased starch content; mid-veins turning pink in severe cases.
diagnostic_features.quote: Infection with SCYLV results in intense yellowing of the midrib, which extends to the leaf blade, followed by tissue necrosis from the leaf tip towards the leaf base. Such symptomatic leaves are usually characterized by increased respiration, reduced photosynthesis, a change in the ratio of hexose to sucrose, and an increase in starch content.
